# Athena

> Athena is a self-hosted code-coverage and CI-insights platform. It ingests the coverage and test reports your CI pipelines produce and turns them into browsable reports per repository, branch, commit, and pull request, so a team can see what its tests actually cover and how that changes over time.

This is the complete Athena documentation in a single file. It describes the web
application — the interface a user interacts with — at the level of user-visible
capability, written from the application's own source at version 25.6.2. It deliberately
does not describe server-side processing, data storage, request or response schemas, or
internal service behavior.

## Overview

### Athena

**Project**: Athena
**Version**: 25.6.2

> Athena is a self-hosted code-coverage and CI-insights platform. It ingests coverage
> and test reports produced by your CI pipelines and turns them into browsable reports
> at the repository, branch, commit, and pull-request level, so teams can see what their
> tests actually cover and how that changes over time.

#### What Athena is for

Athena answers questions a team asks continuously about its own test suite:

- How much of this repository is covered by tests, and which parts are not?
- Did this pull request make coverage better or worse?
- Which files and lines did this commit change, and were those lines tested?
- Which tests are slow, flaky, or failing most often?
- Is the JavaScript bundle we ship getting bigger?

It is a reporting and analysis layer over data your CI already produces. Athena does not
run your tests; your CI runs them and uploads the resulting reports to Athena.

#### How teams use it

1. Connect a source-control organization and pick the repositories to track.
2. Configure the repository so CI uploads its coverage and test reports after each run.
3. Read the results in Athena — per repository, per branch, per commit, per pull request.

Once uploads are flowing, the day-to-day use is mostly reading pull-request and commit
views to see the coverage impact of a change before it merges.

#### Supported source-control providers

Athena signs in against, and reads repository metadata from, the following providers:

- GitHub
- GitLab
- Bitbucket

Athena also supports Okta as an identity provider for organizations that use it.

#### Self-hosted edition

Athena is the self-hosted edition, which changes what the application presents compared
with a hosted subscription product:

- **No subscription, billing, or plan-management screens.** These are absent from the
  self-hosted build rather than merely hidden.
- **No seat-purchase or member-invitation billing flow.** User and access administration
  is handled through the administration area instead.
- **An administration area** is available to administrators for installation-wide
  settings and user administration.
- Sign-in is handled by the deployment's configured identity provider rather than a
  public sign-up page.

#### Scope of this document

This document describes Athena's **web application** — the interface a user interacts
with — at the level of user-visible capability. It is written from the web application's
own source at version 25.6.2.

It deliberately does **not** describe server-side processing, data storage, request or
response schemas, or internal service behavior. Those are not part of the web
application and are not documented here. Where this document says Athena "shows" or
"requests" something, that is a statement about the interface only.

#### Feature inventory

See the feature list for the enumerated, user-visible capabilities and where each one
appears in the interface.

## Features

### Feature List

User-visible capabilities of the Athena web application, version 25.6.2.

Each entry describes what a user can do in the interface. Availability notes reflect the
**self-hosted** build, which omits some screens present in hosted subscription products.

#### Coverage reporting

##### F001 — Repository coverage overview
The main view for a tracked repository: current coverage for the selected branch, a
coverage trend over time, and a browsable file tree showing coverage per directory and
per file. A sunburst-style visualization of coverage distribution is available.

##### F002 — File and line-level coverage
Open any file in a repository and read it with per-line coverage annotation, showing
which lines are covered, uncovered, or partially covered.

##### F003 — Coverage by flag
Break coverage down by upload *flag*, so a repository whose CI uploads several separate
reports (for example unit versus integration, or per language) can be read one slice at
a time rather than only in aggregate.

##### F004 — Coverage by component
Break coverage down by *component* — a named grouping of paths defined in repository
configuration — so ownership-based or subsystem-based coverage can be tracked separately.

##### F005 — Branch selection
Switch the branch a coverage view refers to, and compare the state of coverage between
branches.

#### Change review

##### F006 — Pull request coverage review
For a pull request: whether coverage rose or fell, an indirect-change breakdown, the
files the pull request touched, and per-line coverage on those changes. This is the view
used to judge coverage impact before merging.

##### F007 — Commit detail
For a single commit: its coverage totals, the files it changed, per-line coverage on the
changed lines, and the upload(s) associated with that commit — including whether an
expected upload is missing or failed to process.

##### F008 — Commit history
A list of a repository's commits with their coverage figures, so a regression can be
traced back to the commit that introduced it.

##### F009 — Pull request list
A list of a repository's open and recent pull requests with their coverage status.

#### Bundle analysis

##### F010 — JavaScript bundle reports
Track the size of shipped JavaScript bundles for a repository over time, per branch, and
inspect an individual bundle's composition, so size regressions are visible.

##### F011 — Bundler integration setup
Guided setup for sending bundle data from a project's build, with instructions for
several JavaScript build tools and frameworks, including Webpack, Rollup, Vite,
SvelteKit, Nuxt, Remix, and SolidStart.

#### Test analytics

##### F012 — Test result reporting
Reporting over uploaded test results for a repository — surfacing failure rates, flaky
tests, and slow tests, so an unreliable or expensive test suite can be identified.

#### Repository setup and configuration

##### F013 — Repository onboarding
Instructions for activating a repository and getting its first coverage upload working,
including the upload token needed by CI.

##### F014 — Repository configuration
Per-repository settings, covering general options, the repository's YAML configuration,
and the badges and graphs that can be embedded elsewhere (for example in a README).

##### F015 — Coverage badges and graphs
Generate embeddable coverage badges and graph images for a repository.

#### Organization

##### F016 — Organization repository list
List the repositories in an organization with their coverage state, with search and
filtering to find a repository.

##### F017 — Provider synchronization
Connect and re-synchronize a source-control organization so Athena sees the current set
of repositories and their metadata.

##### F018 — Organization analytics
Aggregate coverage analytics across an organization's repositories, rather than one
repository at a time.

#### Account and administration

##### F019 — Account settings
Per-user account settings, including access tokens and the user's own profile and
session settings.

##### F020 — Installation administration *(self-hosted)*
An administration area, available to administrators, for installation-wide settings and
user administration. This replaces the seat-and-billing member management found in
hosted subscription products.

##### F021 — Seat usage visibility *(self-hosted)*
Visibility into how many of the installation's licensed seats are in use.

#### Optional and conditional features

##### F022 — AI-assisted features *(not enabled by default)*
An AI-assisted area exists in the application but is **disabled by default** and is only
reachable when explicitly enabled for an installation. A default deployment does not
surface it to users.

#### Not present in the self-hosted build

The following are absent from Athena rather than merely hidden, because the self-hosted
build does not include a subscription model:

- Subscription, billing, and plan-management screens.
- Seat-purchase and member-invitation billing flows (see F020 for the administrative
  alternative).
- A public sign-up / sign-in page; sign-in uses the deployment's configured identity
  provider instead.
